segments.he: עוד פ"א הי' בימי מהרנ"ת א' מאנ"ש שהי' קובל צערו לפני מהרנ"ת ז"ל שאחר כל היגיעות וטרחות שמטריח כל היום בשביל פרנסת ב"ב ולבסוף יש לו אשה רעה שבלילה כשבא לנוח היא מחרפת ומגדפת ומקללת אותו והיא עושה לוצרות צרורות. ענה מהרנ"ת ואמר לו בזה"ל: וואזשי ויסטי איך זאל דיר הייסין זיא געטין ווען איך זאל ויסען אז דיא וועסט קריגען אבעסערי מיילא. עס קען דיך אובער זיין אז דיא וועסט קריגען אערגרין שלאק דאס איז איינס, אין ווידערמיר ווייסען דיך אז לא חשיד קוב"ה דעביד דימי בל דינא מן הסתם אזמען ?? ביך קימטער דאסיאיז דיך ?? פארדיר הטובה איידער וען זוול דיך זי דלין אפרעמציר צווישין מענשין אין זוולסט ליידין גרוסי בזיונות איז צורך גלאסער אז דיין אייגען ווייבט זידעלטדיך בא דיר אין שטוב אין קיינשר ווייסט ניט".
segments.en:
On the theme of the foolishness of toiling for livelihood in vain — Rabbainu told a parable: There was once a wealthy man, a great host of guests. Whoever entered his home, they filled his every need — beyond food, drink, and sleep — everything, with a royal open hand. Because of this, all peoples knew of him and everyone came to him — and they left fully satisfied.

Once a certain poor man heard of this generous host. But by bad fortune it happened that he arrived at the door of a certain miser — who had never given even a piece of bread to a poor man — thinking this was the great generous host. He began to bow and scrape with all manner of entreaty, supplication, and honorable words: "Are you not the great noble man of generous heart?" — in order to get food. The miser was astonished and understood that the poor man thought he was the generous host. He said: "Yes, they must give you food — but only a little, and afterward you will repay." And he put him to work: chopping wood, drawing water, all manner of labor — for several hours until the man was exhausted. Afterward he showed him the true generous host's home and said: "Go in there and they will give you food."

The poor man thought this was a second house belonging to the man he had worked for — that after working at the first house, one goes to the second to eat. The moment he entered, servants came out to receive him, washed him, and immediately set the table with all manner of foods and delicacies — all with great honor, as a servant before his master. In the middle of the meal he said: "All this toil was worth it!" The generous host replied: "My dear friend — what toil did you do here with me? You did not toil here at all!" And he told him about the miser he had worked for. The host said: "Ir hot geharvet umzist un ir est umzist — dort voo ir hot geharvet, est ir nit, un dort voo ir est, hot ir nit geharvet" [You toiled in vain and you eat in vain — where you toiled you do not eat, and where you eat you did not toil].

And Rabbainu concluded: "Men arbet umzist un men est umzist — dort voo men arbet, est men nit, un dort voo men est, arbet men nit" [One toils in vain and one eats in vain — where one toils, one does not eat, and where one eats, one has not toiled].

The parable's meaning: when a person toils for his livelihood, he exerts himself at what he thinks his sustenance depends upon — but in truth all comes from Hashem, and when the time designated in Heaven arrives [or when one has prayed and trusted], the sustenance comes easily on its own. All the toil accomplishes nothing — for where one toils, one does not eat [the toil is in the wrong place]. Had he not toiled, the same would have been given to him [for the Giver requires no labor]. As the Zohar says: "They went out and gathered in folly" — those who had faith regarding the manna did not toil at all; it fell into their mouths. But those who lacked faith gathered all day — and in the end had only the same omer per person. And it is written in the holy books that even in our times regarding livelihood this is so — whether one works with crushing effort all day or works only minimally, the designated amount comes. And one who has strong faith and trust in Hashem will certainly find that Hashem provides as desired.
